data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for the better-corroborated theory is defensible on his own terms as a methodological rule of 'risk-minimization' rather than an inductive inference of probability; however, accepting this defense costs the agent any rational assurance that the future will resemble the past, reducing scientific action to a non-rational (though critical) gamble.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the preference for the better-corroborated theory implicitly assigns a higher subjective probability of future success, it collapses into the induction Popper rejected.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If Popper's formal attempt to define verisimilitude (truth-likeness) logically fails, then 'survival of severe tests' cannot serve as a proxy for closeness to truth.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If acting on a theory inherently assumes it will continue to work, then any distinction between 'acting' and 'believing it probable' is merely semantic.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The argument distinguishes between 'justification' (which requires induction) and 'criticism' (which only requires logical falsifiability). It posits that preferring Theory A over Theory B is not a claim that A is more likely true, but a strategic decision that A has withstood tests that would have killed B, making A the 'least error-prone known option' relative to current knowledge. This shifts the ground from epistemic probability to pragmatic survival without assuming uniformity of nature.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
